newsitem.title: JAPAN: Scandal-hit Nomura stands tall against rivals.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit Nomura stands tall against rivals.

text.p: Scandal-tainted Nomura Securities Co Ltd displayed on Thursday its overwhelming strength within the Japanese brokerage industry in its first quarter earnings for the current business year.
Nomura posted 34.93 billion yen ($301 million) in parent current profits for the April-June period, down from 36.42 billion yen ($313 million) a year earlier.
The figures were down year-on-year, but were way above those of its "Big Four" rivals in the industry.
The current profit of Daiwa Securities Co Ltd, the nation's second biggest brokerage, was 15.32 billion yen ($132 million), down from 25.18 billion yen ($217 million) a year earlier.
Current profit is pretax profit and includes gains and losses from non-operating activities.

The third biggest brokerage, Nikko Securities Co Ltd, fell into the red with a parent current loss of 1.93 billion yen ($16.6 million) in the first quarter versus a 19.22 billion yen ($165 million) profit a year earlier.
The fourth biggest brokerage, Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd, is due to announce its quarterly results on Friday and may also post losses, industry sources said.
Nomura's business has been hard hit by revelations of its involvement in a recent racketeer payoff scandal.
However, Nomura's first quarter results confirmed it is still the dominant player in the industry in spite of its weakened credibility.
Many former Nomura executives have been arrested and earlier this week, Japan's securities watchdog urged the finance minister to impose penalties against Nomura.
Corporate clients have shunned Nomura since the scandal broke in March and the top brokerage has been suspended from underwriting government and government-backed bonds.

"While people say that customers have voluntarily suspended their securities business with Nomura, the company's business at the local branch office level has not been damaged so much," Daiwa's managing director Takeshi Nojima told reporters.
Nomura's broking commissions dropped by 38.2 percent year-on-year in the April-to-June quarter, while its underwriting business fell a sharp 78.7 percent.

But its profits in trading activities including foreign exchange transactions and derivatives were 40.46 billion yen ($348 million) in the first quarter against 22.77 billion yen ($196 million) in profits from bond dealings a year earlier.
"We saw an increase in our share of the underwriting business, but that was not much of a gain for us as profit margins in the wholesale business were thin," Nojima said.
Executives at the top three brokerages said that the business results for the first quarter were somewhat irregular as a result of changes in accounting procedures.
Takamichi Arata, a Nomura director, said that the change had helped to boost Nomura's profits.
Daiwa's Nojima also said that first quarter profits rose by an extra six billion yen ($51.7 million) due to a change in accounting procedures.
From the current business year which started in April, Japanese brokerages have been allowed to use mark-to-market accounting methods for derivatives and short-term securities trading.
Previously, financial products were appraised according to the cost at the time of purchase and realised gains or losses were posted in income statements only when positions were closed.

Nomura had unrealised profits of 17 billion yen ($146 million) on trading activities at the end of the last financial year, and the entire amount was included in profits reported for the first quarter, following the change in the accounting procedures, Arata said.

Analysts, however, said that Nomura's earnings would be hit hard in the coming months as the Ministry of Finance will take punitive action against Nomura within a month, with the moves expected to include the suspension of some of its key businesses.
Nomura's Arata said that the company believes the Finance Ministry penalties will affect its earnings. ($1=116 yen)
